name: Aloe Vera
summary: Aloe vera (Aloe barbadensis) is a succulent whose clear inner-leaf gel is used topically for skin and taken orally as a supplement. Its most-studied internal use is blood-sugar control: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials in people with prediabetes or early, untreated type 2 diabetes found that oral aloe vera lowered fasting glucose, with a smaller effect on HbA1c. The included trials were small and used varied preparations, so the evidence is preliminary. The bitter latex layer just under the leaf skin contains aloin, a stimulant laxative, and is not intended for regular ingestion.

safetyNotes: PREPARATION-SPECIFIC SAFETY: Topical inner-leaf aloe gel differs substantially from oral latex, whole-leaf preparations, juice and supplements. Oral aloe latex/anthraquinone laxative preparations can cause severe diarrhea, low potassium and medication interactions; liver injury/hepatitis has been reported with some internal aloe products. MSKCC discourages internal supplement use. The FDA's 2002 determination concerned aloe-containing OVER-THE-COUNTER STIMULANT LAXATIVE DRUG ingredients lacking recognized safety/effectiveness, not a ban on all aloe or topical gel. Avoid oral use during pregnancy; caution with kidney disease, medicines affected by potassium loss and glucose-lowering agents.
contraindications: Oral aloe latex or whole-leaf laxatives: avoid unsupervised use
Oral aloe in kidney disease: avoid without clinician assessment
interactions: Oral latex may interact with diuretics
Oral laxative preparations may lower potassium, creating concern with digoxin, diuretics and corticosteroids
Oral aloe products may affect blood glucose; caution with antidiabetic medicines
